 Some Americans Will Get Their 3.6% Social Security Raise Early - But There's a Catch
 January's SSI payment arrives in December, while Social Security and federal retirement increases follow different rules that could affect your budget.
 By
 Chris Lewis, CEPF 
 ,
 Edited by
 Laura Hohenstein 
 Updated
 Nov. 9, 2026
 Fact checked 
 This article was subjected to a comprehensive fact-checking process. Our professional fact-checkers verify article information against primary sources, reputable publishers, and experts in the field.
 Add Us On Google
 Google Preferred Sources lets you customize your search results. By choosing to follow FinanceBuzz, you’re telling Google to prioritize content from a source you trust.
A higher benefit payment can offer some breathing room when groceries, rent, and insurance already stretch your budget. But an early deposit can also make your bank balance look more comfortable than it really is. 
The Social Security Administration's 2027 cost-of-living adjustment raises the federal Supplemental Security Income (SSI) payment standard by 3.6%. The first higher SSI payment is scheduled for December 31, 2026, because January 1 is a federal holiday. 
That deposit covers January. It isn't a bonus payment or an extra month of benefits. 
The same inflation adjustment also brings higher Social Security benefits and federal retirement annuities, although the amounts, eligibility rules, and payment dates differ. 
 Here's what to know before building the increase into your budget and how you can avoid money mistakes .

 Did you know if your air conditioner stops working, your homeowner’s insurance won’t cover it? Same with plumbing, electrical issues, appliances, and more.

 Your January SSI payment arrives in December
 SSI payments normally arrive on the first of the month. When that date falls on a weekend or federal holiday, SSA schedules the payment for the preceding business day. 
For January 2027, that means Thursday, December 31, 2026. Recipients are therefore scheduled to receive both their regular December payment and their January payment during December, with no regular SSI payment scheduled during January. 
That timing creates the main budget catch. If you spend the December 31 deposit on holiday purchases or December expenses, the money may be gone before January's rent, utilities, or groceries come due. 
If possible, label the deposit as January income and set it aside for that month's bills. Two deposits in December still need to cover two months.

 The federal SSI maximum rises, but your payment may differ
The maximum federal SSI payment increases from $994 to $1,029 per month for an eligible individual in 2027. For an eligible couple, the maximum rises from $1,491 to $1,544. 
Those are increases of $35 and $53, respectively. SSA calculates the new standards using unrounded annual amounts, then rounds the monthly figures down to whole dollars. 
Your actual payment may differ from those maximums. SSA subtracts countable income when calculating benefits, and some states provide supplemental payments. That means multiplying your current deposit by 3.6% may not give you the correct new amount. 
Use your official benefit notice to confirm what you should receive, especially if your income or living arrangement has changed. 
 Social Security's average increase is about $75
Social Security retirement benefits also receive a 3.6% COLA, beginning with payments received in January 2027. SSA estimates that the average retired-worker benefit will rise from $2,095 to $2,170 per month, an increase of about $75 before deductions. 
That figure is an average, rather than a flat increase for everyone. A $1,500 gross monthly benefit would rise by approximately $54, while a $2,500 benefit would rise by approximately $90. 
If you receive both SSI and Social Security, keep the payment schedules separate. The January SSI payment is scheduled for December 31, while your Social Security payment follows its applicable January schedule. 
Also, don't assume the two increases simply add together. Social Security counts toward SSI's countable-income calculation, so a higher Social Security benefit can affect how much SSI you receive.

 Medicare and taxes can reduce the Social Security gain
For beneficiaries whose Medicare premiums are deducted from Social Security, higher deductions can leave less of the gross COLA available to spend. 
The useful comparison is the change in deductions. For example, a $75 gross benefit increase paired with a $12 increase in Medicare deductions would leave $63 more before any other changes. 
Higher income can also affect Medicare surcharges. Income-related monthly adjustment amounts, known as IRMAA, generally use tax information from two years earlier. Your 2027 surcharge would therefore generally reflect your 2025 income, rather than your new 2027 COLA . 
Taxes require a separate distinction. SSI payments aren't subject to federal income tax. Social Security benefits can be taxable, with up to 85% included in taxable income depending on your combined income and filing status. That is the share subject to tax, rather than an 85% tax rate. 
If you elected federal tax withholding from Social Security, compare the old and new withholding amounts when reviewing your deposit. 
 Federal retirees face a different COLA formula
Federal retirement annuities have their own rules. Eligible Civil Service Retirement System annuitants receive a 3.6% COLA for 2027, while eligible Federal Employees Retirement System annuitants generally receive 2.6%. 
FERS also generally restricts COLAs before age 62, with exceptions for certain disability, survivor, and special-category benefits. Recent retirees may receive a prorated first adjustment. 
The federal annuity COLA takes effect December 1 and appears in the January payment covering December. New-year health coverage changes follow a different timetable: FEHB changes for annuitants take effect January 1, with the premium deduction generally reflected in February's annuity payment. 
That makes it useful to review both payments before deciding how much more you can spend each month. 
 Other assistance may need a separate review
If you receive SSI alongside other income-based assistance, check how that program handles benefit increases. 
For SNAP, states have procedures to account for Social Security and SSI COLAs through benefit adjustments. The effect on your household depends on the applicable calculation, so review your agency's notice before assuming your food assistance will stay the same. 
Follow the reporting instructions for each program. A change handled automatically by one agency may still require attention elsewhere. 
 Retirement News: Almost 80% of Americans fear a retirement age increase — here’s the real reason why 
 Bottom line
The first higher SSI payment arrives December 31, but it needs to cover January. Keeping that distinction clear can help prevent an early deposit from turning into a budget shortfall. 
Check your official notice for the actual amount. If you also receive Social Security or a federal annuity, review each benefit separately, including its payment date, eligibility rules, and deductions. 
The COLA can help with rising costs and is important to know for your retirement plan . Plan around the money available for each month's bills, and give January's early SSI payment its intended job. 
 FAQs
 Why is January's SSI payment arriving in December?
 The first SSI payment reflecting the 3.6% COLA is scheduled for Dec. 31, 2026. It arrives early because January 1 is a federal holiday, but the money covers January's benefits. It isn't an extra payment.
 How much will SSI payments increase in 2027?
 The maximum federal monthly payment rises to $1,029 for an eligible individual and $1,544 for an eligible couple. Your actual amount depends on countable income and any state supplement, so check your benefit notice before budgeting around the maximum.
 Will everyone receiving SSI get the same increase?
 No. The COLA raises the federal payment standard, but SSA subtracts countable income when calculating your benefit. Changes in other income can affect your payment, so multiplying your current deposit by 3.6% may not produce the correct amount.
